title: Searching for the ox
hookLine: the ten oxherding pictures: first, a herdsman searches for a lost ox

cards: A man stands at the edge of a field of wild grass, a rope in his hand. The grass is high. Beyond it, a river, and past the river, mountains.
Somewhere out there is his ox, and it's gone. He pushes through the grass, crosses the water, climbs, and keeps going until the paths blur together and his legs give out. Evening comes.
Nothing. No ox, no hoofprint, just cicadas in the trees as the light goes. That's the whole of the first picture in a series Chan and Zen have used to draw the way itself.

teach.b: The oxherding pictures this path follows are a set of ten images, each with a short prose preface and a short poem. Tradition credits this set to a Chan teacher named Kuoan, known in Japan as Kakuan.
They follow a herdsman and his ox from loss, through finding and taming, all the way home and beyond, and over the coming days this path walks them one at a time.

teach.h: THE FIRST: ALONE IN TALL GRASS.
teach.b: The first poem, in paraphrase: busily parting the endless grasses, he searches. The rivers are wide, the mountains far, the path keeps going. Worn out, he finds nothing, and hears only the cicadas in the evening maples.
Effort, with no result yet. Then the twist, in the preface.
In paraphrase: the ox has never gone missing.
So why search? Because the herdsman turned his back on awakening, the ox became a stranger to him and got lost in the dust.
Far from home, he stands at a crossroads, and gain and loss flare up in him like fire, right and wrong like a thicket of spears.
Some readers hear the ox as the herdsman's own true nature: never really gone, only turned away from. Why start here?
It would be easy to skip this picture and want the finding. But the first step is admitting the search is on, and naming it. Everything that follows begins with someone out in the grass, looking.

how: Some Zen and Chan teachers use the oxherding pictures in talks and retreats as a map of practice, and students often study the pictures, prefaces and poems one stage at a time.

games.q: what does “searching for the ox” mean?
o: a farmer's prayer for a lost animal's return
a herdsman hunting an ox that was never lost
a later picture, where the ox is ridden home

p: the ox has never gone missing
tradition credits him with one set

s: the first picture's preface says the ox was never really lost
the herdsman turned his back on awakening, and so the ox became a stranger.
the first picture shows the herdsman leading the ox home

games.q: you've searched through grass, across rivers, up into the mountains, until your legs give out. what does the first picture show you finding?
o: nothing yet, only cicadas as night comes
a map left by another herdsman
games.why: the first picture ends with no ox at all. its preface adds the twist: the ox was never really lost.

practice: Ask yourself gently: what am I searching for? Not the polished answer, the real one, peace or approval or rest or something without a name yet; when it comes, name it simply, in a word or two, and don't argue with it.
Then let the question go and rest with the breath, the way the herdsman might finally sit down at dusk and listen to the cicadas.

wordCard.voice: Searching for the ox. The first of the oxherding pictures: a herdsman alone in the grasses, looking for an ox the preface says was never lost. Today's word.
